summary: Extends the postmaster concept to X.400 mail domains that have registered RFC 1327 mapping rules and therefore appear to have normal RFC 822-style addresses. It was proposed as a standard. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1648 extends the postmaster-address convention to X.400 domains that map to RFC 822-style addresses. A domain that accepts mapped user addresses must also make its postmaster address work.

questions: how to support postmaster in x.400
what is the x.400 postmaster convention
why must an x.400 domain support postmaster
where should postmaster mail be routed
subtitle: A convention for supporting postmaster addresses in mapped X.400 mail domains.

tldr.problem: An X.400 domain can have RFC 822-style mapped addresses even when mail to postmaster at that domain is not deliverable.
tldr.mechanism: For each mapped domain with valid user addresses, the corresponding Postmaster X.400 address must also be valid and routed to someone responsible for mail or site operations.
tldr.outcome: The RFC extends the postmaster convention to mapped X.400 domains; the unit metadata marks it Historic.

today: The unit metadata marks RFC 1648 as Historic. The RFC records a convention for postmaster addresses in X.400 domains with RFC 1327 mappings.

sections.title: Why a Postmaster Address Matters
sections.content:
Mail and system managers may need to contact someone responsible for a remote mail system without knowing a particular user's address. RFC 822 and the Internet Host Requirements therefore require the address postmaster at Internet hosts.

X.400 domains with RFC 1327 mapping rules can appear to use ordinary RFC 822-style email addresses. If a mapped user address works but the mapped postmaster address does not, remote operators may have no way to report a problem.
sections.plainLanguage: A postmaster address gives people a way to contact someone responsible for a mail system. Mapped X.400 domains need that address to work too.

sections.title: The X.400 Postmaster Convention
sections.content:
For an X.400 domain with an RFC 1327 mapping rule, if any address of the form user@domain is valid, then postmaster@domain must also be valid. In X.400 terms, the corresponding address uses Surname=Postmaster with the same remaining address elements.

For X.400(1988), the document also says CommonName=Postmaster must be supported. Mail to the postmaster is routed to someone responsible for the site's mail system or general site operation.
sections.plainLanguage: If a mapped X.400 domain accepts mail for users, it must also accept mail for postmaster. That message goes to someone responsible for mail or site operations.

sections.title: Supporting Older X.400 Software
sections.content:
The RFC encourages X.400 software developers to support forwarding postmaster mail to a central mailbox. It says software that cannot meet the requirement should be upgraded.

As possible workarounds, the memo mentions creating a postmaster mailing list with one destination, using X.400 autoforwarding, or rewriting the address in another way.
sections.plainLanguage: Software can route postmaster mail to a central mailbox. The RFC also describes mailing lists, autoforwarding, and address rewriting as possible workarounds.
